L475@P16: Smaller clusters of incised steatite tablets as well as multiple copies
L476@P16: from the same general area have been found previously at Harappa, notably
L477@P16: in Trench I of Mound F (Vats 1940). What is particularly important about
L478@P16: the specimens from Trench 11, however, is that because of the nature of
L479@P16: the excavation it is possible to show that they all come from contemporary
L480@P16: or nearly contemporary stratigraph.ic units, and it seems likely that although
L481@P16: made by different hands they derived from a single source. But whatever
L482@P16: value or use they may havc had when they were made had clearly been
L483@P16: lost by the time they were deposited together with other debris on the
L484@P16: outside of the Mound E perimeter wall. Of great interest in this regard is a
L485@P16: unicorn seal (Fig. 4.1) that was found inside the perimeter wall in the
L486@P16: approximate location marked in Fig. 2 (no. 1). The last two signs of this
L487@P16: seal are the same as those on one side of the 22 tablets (taking the three
L488@P16: strokes as a single sign). These are preceded by three additional signs (reading
L489@P16: left to right on the seal as opposed to on the tablets which we assume are
L490@P16: meant to be read right to left because they were not meant to be impressed
L491@P16: - see endnote 3). It is rare to find the same sign sequence on a seal and on
L492@P16: tablets, and the situation is that much more compelling because the street
L493@P16: deposits from which the seal comes contain the same ceramic corpus as
L494@P16: the dump deposits from which the tablets come, suggesting that both were
L495@P16: originally formed at about the same time.
L496@P16: It is tempting to think that the evident loss of utility and subsequent
L497@P16: discard of the tablets is relatcd to the 'death' of the seal. Seals are almost
L498@P16: always found in trash or street deposits (and never yet in a grave) indicating
L499@P16: that they were either lost or intentionally discarded, the latter seeming the
L500@P16: more likely in most instances. The end ofthe utility of a seal must relate to
L501@P16: some life event of its owner, whether change of status, or death, or the
L502@P16: passing of an amount oftime during which the seal was considered current.

L169@P4: tablets usually reflect a more formal use of the script while those on other artifacts may be

L171@P4: Spontaneity is particularly likely for graffiti on ceramic vessels, which were incised with script
L172@P4: after manufacturing and firing. This use of signs clearly demonstrates that it was not only
L173@P4: craftsmen commissioned to prepare formal devices who incised the script, but also others who
L174@P4: employed it directly to label a container with perhaps one or more of the following: the name
L175@P4: of its owner, the nature of its contents, its origin, its destination, or an incantation – to name
L176@P4-5: some of the more obvious possibilities. Regrettably, most examples of ceramic vessels with incised signs are broken, with the inscription only partially preserved on the recovered sherd(s). 6 J. MARK KENOYER & RICHARD H. MEADOW
L177@P5: This provides a challenge in trying to investigate what degree of overlap there may be in sign
L178@P5: sequences between graffiti and inscriptions on seals, tablets, or other media.
L179@P5: Much of our recent work at Harappa has focused on understanding the details of cultural
L180@P5: developments during Periods 3B and 3C. Results reveal these to have been dynamic periods of
L181@P5: urban expansion together with recurrent decay, rebuilding, and reorganization in different
L182@P5: parts of the city. In 2000 and 2001, excavations turned to recovering more information on
L183@P5: Period 3A in order to reveal initial Harappa Phase developments, particularly relating to the
L184@P5: use of inscribed pieces. This period is poorly represented in excavations at most Indus sites,
L185@P5: because the remains are buried under later occupation levels. At Harappa, it has been possible
L186@P5: to recover two seal fragments from Period 3A, providing an important baseline against which
L187@P5: to evaluate stylistic and technological change in the use of seals (see below for more discussion). Based on evidence at hand to date, square seals with script together with the unicorn or
L188@P5: other animal motifs are associated primarily with the later part of Period 3A and are relatively
L189@P5: common throughout Period 3B and on into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997). Square
L190@P5: seals with script alone are found first in Period 3B, but long rectangular seals with script alone
L191@P5: are confined to Period 3C.
L192@P5: We are also obtaining important chronological information with respect to inscribed tablets, which are particularly common at Harappa, more so than the seals. Through careful stratigraphic cutting-back of Vats’ section in Trench I of Mound F and comparison with his report
L193@P5: of that trench (Vats 1940), we have determined that he was not correct in reporting that small
L194@P5: steatite tablets with incised script are from the earliest levels of the site. Instead it is evident
L195@P5: that such tablets appeared toward the middle of Period 3B and continued to be used well into
L196@P5: Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997; 2000). Furthermore, these inscribed steatite tablets,
L197@P5: which Vats (1940) called “tiny steatite seals”, are not seals at all but are incised with script
L198@P5: that was to be read directly from the tablet. And along with the steatite tablets are found terracotta and glazed faience tablets with molded bas-relief script, motifs, and narrative scenes,
L199@P5: which also start appearing in mid-Period 3B and continue into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer
L200@P5: 1997; 2000).
L201@P5: While many of the tablets are rectangular in form, others were made in circular, half circle, or fan shapes and even in the form of trees, fish, hares, or other animals. Most tablets are
L202@P5: flat in cross-section, but others are triangular, deeply rectangular to square, plano-convex, biconvex, or almost cylindrical (e.g., this volume: H-1956 & H-1957 and H-1979, H-1980 & H1981). This last form has led to much confusion in the literature as they are often incorrectly
L203@P5: referred to as cylinder seals. So far, no true cylinder seals have been recovered from the HARP
L204@P5: excavations, although the Central Asian type of cylinder seal is reported from earlier excavations and from other sites (Parpola 1994).
L205@P5: Unlike seals, almost all of which are unique, an important aspect of tablets is that, at
L206@P5: Harappa (as well as at Mohenjo-daro), there are numerous instances of (1) incised steatite
L207@P5: tablets with copies of the same signs and/or motifs and (2) duplicate bas-relief tablets of
L208@P5: faience or terracotta made from the same mold (e.g., Meadow & Kenoyer 2000). The molds
L209@P5: themselves could have been made of wood or clay or stone, and seem also to have included
L210@P5: seals (e.g., this volume: H-1130 through H-1132 and H-1951A).8 Copies of incised tablets and

L216@P6: duplicates of molded tablets have been found in large numbers in two noteworthy instances at
L217@P6: Harappa: (1) script copies incised into 22 rectangular steatite tablets, triangular in section,
L218@P6: from secondary deposits of Period 3B on the outside of the perimeter wall in Trench 11 on
L219@P6: the East side of Mound E (Meadow & Kenoyer 2000, fig. 4; this volume: H-2218 through
L220@P6: H-2239) and (2) 31 duplicates bearing iconography and script, made of rectangular molded
L221@P6: terracotta, biconvex in section, from the northern portion of Trench II in Area G (Vats 1940:
L222@P6: 195; CISI 1: H-252 through H-265 and H-276 & H-277; CISI 2: H-859 through H-870; this
L223@P6: volume: H-1155). Other copies and duplicates have been found scattered across the site where,
L224@P6: like the multiples above, they are always found in trash, fill, or street deposits. Why tablets
L225@P6: were made, how they were used, and why they were discarded remain intriguing unanswered
L226@P6: questions. Their intrinsic interest lies not only in the script that they often bear, but even more
L227@P6: so in the iconography, which provides an important glimpse, however fragmentary, into details
L228@P6: of Harappan ideology, particularly for the time frame from ca. 2400 to ca. 2000 BC (Harappa
L229@P6: Period 3B through much of Period 3C). For a more detailed discussion see Meadow &
